respective

/rih-SPEK-tiv/ — stress on second syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Respective describes something that belongs individually to each particular person or thing in a group, rather than being shared.

After the ceremony, the teams returned to their respective locker rooms.

Example

After the championship debate, the three teams collected their respective trophies—Team A took the gold, Team B took the silver, and Team C took the bronze.

Respective is more precise than just 'their own' because it emphasizes that each trophy is individually assigned to its particular team, not mixed or shared. The word clarifies the one-to-one matching: each team gets its specific trophy. Plain 'their own' would work, but respective highlights the individual assignment.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

own: Own means belonging to that person alone — my own room, your own idea. It stresses possession and nothing else. Respective adds a different job: with a whole group and a list of things, it matches each member to the one that is theirs, in order.

particular: Particular means specific to one certain person or thing — it picks one item out of the crowd, as in 'that particular book.' Respective does not single anything out; it works across a whole group at once, pairing every member with the thing that corresponds to it.

individual: Individual means meant for each single member separately, rather than for the group as a whole — individual portions, individual scores. Respective goes one step further than keeping things separate: it lines two lists up and matches each person to the specific item that is theirs.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

shared: belonging to everyone in the group together

collective: owned or done by the whole group as one

Where it sits · how strictly things are matched one-to-one

common property → shared belongings → own stuff → respective

common property vs. respective: Common property belongs to everyone at once — the opposite of items going to their respective owners.

shared belongings vs. respective: Shared belongings get used by the whole group together, while respective possessions are matched one-to-one to each person.

own stuff vs. respective: 'Own stuff' casually says things belong to someone, but respective formally matches each item to its own particular owner.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-: back, again (Latin)

Root — spect: to look (from Latin specere, 'to look')

Suffix — -ive: tending to; having the quality of (Latin -ivus)

Put it together: Re- ('back') + spect ('to look,' from Latin specere) + -ive: Latin respicere meant 'to look back at' — to give each thing its own regard, one at a time. Respective describes things considered individually: each item looked at and matched to its own person.

Use the root in a new word: respectively: Maya and Jon won first and second prize, respectively — Maya took the gold and Jon the silver.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal

Respective is useful in formal or structured situations where each person or thing is being individually assigned or matched to something specific—think team assignments, seating charts, job titles, or official categories. In everyday contexts where people simply have their own stuff, plain 'own' or 'their own' is usually the simpler, better choice. Respective sounds formal on purpose; use it when the situation is formal or when the individual matching is the point.
